blocks.md: This lesson covers the book's section on **Collection Policy Coverage**. Read the excerpt, then test yourself below.

blocks.source: Vol IV, Physical Data, § Collection Policy Coverage
blocks.md: Every logged latch record carries an ingestion cost, an attributed action label, and a hardware timestamp, yet those fields say nothing about which physical situations the archive covers. In an illustrative contact task where a gripper aligns with a workpiece edge across contact angles GripperContactAngle in [-15.0^circ, +15.0^circ] and normal forces up to \$20.0 N, binning at \$1.0^circ and \$1.0 N forms an operational grid of 600 discrete cells. Suppose two collection policies each record \$1,000,000 transitions at \$100 Hz with identical sensors.

blocks.prompt: Think first: In two or three sentences, explain why Scenario coverage table matters for the system this section describes.
blocks.md: Compare your answer with the book's claim: A scenario table enumerates the cells the declared domain requires over low-dimensional task invariants, because a brute-force state grid is defeated by dimensionality.

questions.q: The section **Collection Policy Coverage** develops one of the chapter's claims. Which one?
options: Cartesian labels recorded on one arm can force a different arm through a singularity or drop a redundant degree of freedom, so action spaces transfer only through the embodiment contract.
Teleoperation loop latency is display plus human plus command plus mechanics time, dominated by operator reaction, and it leaves step-and-wait artifacts in the labels.
A scenario table enumerates the cells the declared domain requires over low-dimensional task invariants, because a brute-force state grid is defeated by dimensionality.
Autocorrelated telemetry carries about N(1-rho)/(1+rho) independent samples, so a higher logger rate cannot populate an unvisited cell.

questions.explanation: This section develops **Scenario coverage table**: A scenario table enumerates the cells the declared domain requires over low-dimensional task invariants, because a brute-force state grid is defeated by dimensionality.
